Online Portfolio Building: Show Your Best Work and Win Clients
Build and share a free online portfolio, with clear photos and honest case studies, that turns visitors into customers or job interviews.

Learn to choose your strongest work, photograph physical pieces well with a phone, and write short case studies that explain the problem, your process and the result. When you tell someone "I am a good tailor" or "I design beautiful flyers", you are asking them to trust your word. When you show them five finished pieces, each with a short story of what the customer needed and what you delivered, they can judge for themselves. An **online portfolio** is a single place on the internet, reached with one link, where you show your best work with that context. It works for you while you sleep, and it often does the persuading before you ever speak to the person.

Portfolio, CV or WhatsApp status?

Many skilled women already share their work on WhatsApp status, Instagram or Facebook. That is useful, but it is not the same as a portfolio. A status disappears after 24 hours. A social media feed mixes your best work with your weakest, with greetings, adverts and personal photos, and a new visitor has to scroll for a long time to understand what you do. A **CV** (curriculum vitae) lists your jobs, training and dates, but it describes your work instead of showing it.

You do not have to choose one. A strong set-up is a social media page for regular posting, a CV for job applications, and a portfolio link that you put in both, so that a serious enquirer can see your best work in two minutes.
Who opens your portfolio

Think about the real person on the other side. For a caterer it may be a bride planning her wedding, or an office manager buying lunch packs for a training. For a graphic designer it may be a church media team or a small business owner. For someone looking for employment it may be a hiring manager comparing twenty applicants. Each of them is busy and has a decision to make. They usually spend a short time on a first look before deciding whether to read more or close the page.
Whoever they are, they quietly ask four questions:
**Can she do what I need?** They look for work similar to their own job.
**Is the quality good enough?** They look closely at photos, finishing and detail.
**Can I trust her?** They look for real customers, results, testimonials and a real name and face.
**How do I reach her and what will it cost?** They look for a clear contact button and a guide to your services or starting prices.

The parts of a good portfolio
**A short introduction:** your name, what you do, where you work and who you serve, in one or two sentences.
**Your best work:** usually five to eight pieces, not everything you have ever made.
**A case study for each main piece:** what the customer needed, how you did it, and what happened.
**Proof from other people:** testimonials or reviews, used with permission.
**Services and how to start:** what you offer, and a starting price or "prices from" guide if you are comfortable sharing it.
**Contact:** a WhatsApp button, an email address, and your town or area.
Worked example: the same tailor, two ways of showing her work
For example, Ngozi is a tailor in Enugu. A new customer asks to see her work before ordering an aso ebi outfit for a wedding.
Before: Ngozi forwards 37 photos from her phone gallery in one WhatsApp message. Some are blurry, some show other people's tailoring she saved for ideas, and none say what the customer asked for.
The customer scrolls for a few minutes, cannot tell which pieces are Ngozi's own, and says she will "get back to you".

After: Ngozi sends one link to a simple free website with six pieces. Each has three clear photos (front, back, detail of the beading) and four short lines: the occasion, what the customer wanted, how long it took, and the customer's comment.
The page ends with "Prices from approximately ₦25,000 for a fitted gown, depending on fabric and design" and a button that opens a WhatsApp chat with her.

The customer can now answer all four questions on her own. She messages Ngozi with the exact style she likes and asks for a fitting date. The portfolio did the selling; the conversation is now about details.
It is not only for designers

Portfolios are often linked with graphic designers and photographers, but any work that produces a visible result can be shown: hairstyles, makeup, cakes and small chops, event decoration, soap and skincare products, beadwork, interior arrangements, written articles, social media pages you managed, training you delivered, or a spreadsheet system you set up for a business.

Write down, in one sentence, who your portfolio is for and what you want them to do. For example: "Women in Lekki planning parties who should message me on WhatsApp to book decoration." Or: "NGO hiring managers who should invite me for an interview as a programme assistant." Every choice in the rest of this course, from which pieces to include to which words to use, will be checked against that sentence.

Choosing your strongest and most relevant work
Apply the quality and relevance test to every piece you are considering
Reduce a large collection of work to five to eight strong pieces
Use clearly labelled practice work when you do not yet have paid work
Order your chosen pieces so the best and most relevant come first

The most common portfolio mistake is showing too much. When a viewer sees thirty pieces of mixed quality, she does not remember the best ten. She remembers the weakest three, and she wonders whether that is what she will get. A short, strong selection says: "Everything I show you is my real standard." A useful rule of thumb is **five to eight pieces** for a beginner portfolio. You can add more later in separate sections once each section is strong.
A woman sorting photos into groups on a large screen
Choosing work is mostly about removing pieces, so the ones that remain are all strong.
Two questions for every piece

Look at each piece and ask two separate questions. First, **quality**: is this among my best work? Is the finishing clean, is the photo clear, would I be proud if a demanding customer saw it? Second, **relevance**: does this match the work I want more of, and the person in my portfolio goal? A beautiful wedding cake is high quality, but it is less relevant if your goal is to sell lunch packs to offices.

Only pieces in the top-right box go straight into your portfolio; the others are removed, redone or kept for a different section.

Pieces in the bottom-right box are the most useful to notice. They show the kind of work you want, but the photo or finishing lets you down. Often the fix is simple: make the item again for a friend at cost price, or re-photograph it properly (Module 2 shows you how).
Show range, not repetition

If all six pieces are almost the same, a viewer learns only one thing about you. Within your chosen focus, try to show a range: different occasions, sizes, budgets, colours or customer types. A hairstylist might show knotless braids, a natural hair twist-out, a bridal updo and a children's style. A writer might show a blog article, a product description, a newsletter and a social media caption series. Range tells the viewer you can handle her job, even if it is slightly different from what she sees.
When you do not have much paid work yet

Everyone starts somewhere. If you have little real customer work, you can create **practice pieces** (also called self-initiated or spec work). Make them as close to real jobs as you can, and always label them honestly.
**Self-set briefs:** design a menu for a real type of business, such as a buka in your area, without claiming they hired you. Label it "Practice project".
**Work for family, friends or your church:** these are real projects. Describe them truthfully, for example "Decoration for my sister's 30th birthday, 40 guests."
**Training projects:** work from a course, including this one, labelled as course work.
**Volunteer work:** a poster for a community health day, a WhatsApp group you managed for a women's association.
Never present someone else's work as yours

Do not use photos from Pinterest, Instagram or a supplier's catalogue in your portfolio, even as "examples of what I can do". Customers do find out, often by doing a reverse image search, and one discovered copy can destroy the trust your whole portfolio is meant to build. Keep inspiration pictures in a private folder only.
Worked example: from 40 photos to 6 pieces

For example, Amaka bakes and decorates cakes in Abuja. Her goal: "Mothers planning children's birthday parties in Abuja who should message me to order a themed cake." Her phone has 40 cake photos from two years.
She removes 9 photos that are blurry or taken at night under yellow bulbs: 31 left.
She removes 7 that are other bakers' cakes saved for ideas: 24 left.
She groups the rest: 14 children's birthday cakes, 6 wedding cakes, 4 cupcake boxes.

From the 14 children's cakes she scores each from 1 to 5 for finishing and photo quality, and keeps the five that score 4 or 5. They cover different themes: a football cake, a princess cake, a number cake, a two-tier cartoon cake and a simple cake for a one-year-old.
She adds one cupcake box because many mothers order cupcakes with the cake.
She notes that her best unicorn cake has a poor photo, so she plans to bake a small version and photograph it in daylight.

Amaka's portfolio has six strong, relevant pieces in a sensible order, with one improvement planned. Her wedding cakes are not wasted: they can become a separate section later, when she has five good ones.
Order matters

Viewers give the most attention to the first things they see. Put your **strongest and most relevant** piece first, your second strongest last (people also remember endings), and the others in between. If a piece is there mainly to show range, it can sit in the middle. Write your chosen list in order with one line explaining why each one made it in; you will use those notes when you write case studies.

Gathering material safely: permission, privacy and honest labels

Before you publish anything, check that you are allowed to show it and that it does not expose anyone's private information. A portfolio is public. Anyone with the link can see it, save the pictures and forward them. Being careful here protects your customers, protects you, and shows the professionalism that serious clients look for.
A person next to a padlock and a login screen
A public portfolio needs the same care with private information as any other online account.
Ask permission, and keep it in writing

When the work shows a customer's face, name, home, business or event, ask before you publish. A WhatsApp message is enough, and it gives you a written record. Ask early, ideally when the job is delivered and the customer is happy.
Worked example: a permission message that works
For example, Funke runs a small catering business in Ibadan. She has just delivered small chops and jollof rice for a client's naming ceremony and the client is pleased.

Funke sends: "Thank you for trusting me with your ceremony, Mrs Ade. I am building an online portfolio of my work. May I show 3 photos of the food trays (no guests' faces) and quote your kind message? I can use your first name only, or no name at all, whichever you prefer."
Mrs Ade replies: "Yes, use the photos. First name is fine."
Funke screenshots the reply and saves it in a folder called Permissions, with the date.
She crops out the corner of one photo where a guest's face appears.
Funke has clear, written permission, she has respected the customer's choice about her name, and she has a record if anyone questions it later.

If a customer says no, respect it. You can still describe the job in words ("Catering for a 150-guest corporate end-of-year party in Ibadan") without photos, or show photos with all identifying details removed only if the customer agrees to that.
Protect private details
Look closely at every image before it goes online. Phone photos often capture more than you notice.

Run every image through this check before you upload it.
**Screenshots of chats or reviews:** blur or cover the customer's name, number and profile photo unless they agreed to be named.
**Children:** do not show a child's face without the parent's clear permission. For a children's party, photograph the cake, decor or outfit, not the child.
**Business documents:** if you show a spreadsheet, report or design you made for a company, replace real figures and names with sample data, or get written permission.
**Location:** many phones save the place a photo was taken inside the file. Upload sites often remove it, but to be safe you can turn off location for your camera app in your phone settings.
Your own safety too

Show your town or area (for example, "Surulere, Lagos"), not your full home address. Use a business WhatsApp number if you have one. Never put your BVN, NIN, bank account login, or ID card on a portfolio. Customers need your phone number or email to contact you and your account number only at the point of payment, sent privately.

Nigeria has a data protection law, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, which sets rules for how personal information about people is collected and shared. You do not need to be a lawyer to build a portfolio. The simple habits in this lesson, asking permission and removing personal details, are the right starting point.
Should you add a watermark?

A watermark is your name or logo placed lightly on a photo, so that if someone forwards or copies it, your name travels with it. A small, semi-transparent name in one corner is reasonable for photos of physical products. Avoid large logos across the middle of the picture: they hide the very detail the viewer wants to judge. Remember that a watermark discourages copying but cannot stop it, so the real protection is posting only what you are happy for the public to see.

Guided Practice: Photos, Case Studies and a Free Site

You take clear phone photos of physical work, write short case studies that explain the problem, your process and the result, and build your portfolio on a free tool such as Google Sites, a Canva website, Behance or your LinkedIn Featured section.
Photographing physical work with your phone
Set up soft natural light and a plain background at home at little or no cost
Take a standard set of shots for each piece: overall, detail, scale and in use
Use phone camera features (focus, exposure, gridlines) and avoid common mistakes
Make simple edits without changing the true colour of the work

For physical work such as clothes, cakes, hairstyles, beadwork, soap or décor, the photo is the work as far as an online viewer is concerned. A great outfit in a dark, blurry photo looks like an average outfit. The good news is that you do not need a professional camera. A modern smartphone, daylight from a window and a sheet of white paper or cloth can produce clean, honest photos.
A person photographing a product on a simple tabletop set-up
A plain background and soft daylight are enough for clear portfolio photos.
Light: the most important thing
**Use daylight from a window or door.** Place the item close to the window, with the light coming from the side. Side light shows texture, such as stitching, beading or icing.
**Avoid harsh midday sun.** Direct sun makes hard shadows and burns out white areas. A bright but cloudy day, or a window without direct sun, gives soft light.
**Turn off ceiling bulbs.** Mixing yellow indoor bulbs with daylight gives strange colours.
**Do not use the flash.** It flattens texture and creates shiny spots on glossy items like soap, glass or satin.
**Bounce light into shadows.** Hold a sheet of white paper, a white plate or a piece of foil-covered cardboard on the side opposite the window to lighten the dark side.
Background and set-up

Keep the background plain so that the eye goes to your work. For small items, bend an A4 or larger sheet of white card so it curves from the table up the wall behind; this smooth curve hides the line where table meets wall. For larger items, use a plain wall, a bedsheet or a length of plain fabric. For clothing, a plain wall and a person or a dress form shows how the garment hangs far better than laying it on a bed.

The shot list for each piece
Take more than one photo of each piece. A viewer wants to see the whole thing and the quality up close. For most items, aim for four kinds of shot:
**Overall:** the whole item, straight on, filling most of the frame.
**Detail:** close up on the part that shows skill, such as a hem, beadwork, piping on a cake or a soap swirl.
**Scale:** something that shows size, such as a hand holding the item or a cake beside a cake knife.
**In use:** the item being worn, served, displayed or used. For hairstyles and makeup, the back and side as well as the front.
Camera habits that make a difference
**Wipe the lens** with a soft clean cloth. Phone lenses collect finger grease, which makes photos look hazy.
**Tap the screen on your item** to focus. On most phones you can then slide up or down to make the picture brighter or darker.
**Turn on gridlines** in your camera settings. They help you keep edges straight and the item centred.
**Move closer instead of zooming.** Digital zoom lowers quality; walk closer or use the phone's dedicated zoom lens if it has one.
**Hold still.** Rest your elbows on a table or use a cheap phone tripod, and take several shots so at least one is sharp.
Worked example: a bead necklace shoot
For example, Grace makes bead necklaces in Port Harcourt. She wants six clean photos for her portfolio and spends nothing except approximately ₦300 on a sheet of white cardboard.
At about 10 a.m. she sets a small table next to her window, out of direct sun, and curves the white card against the wall.
She switches off the room bulb and holds a white plate on the shadow side to soften shadows.
She lays the necklace on the card and takes the overall shot from directly above, using gridlines to centre it.
She takes a detail shot of the clasp and the bead pattern, tapping to focus on the beads.
Her sister wears the necklace against a plain wall for an in-use shot, showing how it sits on the neck.
She takes 15 photos in total and keeps the sharpest four.
Grace now has four consistent, bright photos showing the full design, the fine work, the size and the look when worn. The total time was about 30 minutes.
Edit lightly and honestly

Free apps such as **Snapseed** (from Google) or the editor built into your phone's gallery are enough. Crop to remove clutter, straighten the picture, and adjust brightness a little. Do not change colours so much that the customer receives something that looks different from the photo: if the fabric is wine, it should look wine, not red. Do not use beauty filters that change the shape of a hairstyle or a face in makeup work.
Save data and space

Very large photo files load slowly on a viewer's phone and use up her data. Most portfolio tools resize images for you, but if a site asks you to upload smaller files, use your gallery's resize or a free compression option. Keep the original, full-size photo in your Google Drive folder.

Writing case studies: problem, process and result
Structure a case study with a title, the problem, your process and the result
Write each part in short, specific sentences of everyday language
Describe results honestly, with real numbers or the customer's own words
Adapt the length of a case study to how important the piece is

A photo shows what you made. A **case study** explains why it was needed, how you did it and what difference it made. That story is what turns "nice picture" into "she understands my kind of problem". Case studies are especially important for work that cannot be judged from a picture alone, such as writing, social media management, admin systems or training, but they help every kind of portfolio.
A woman writing notes beside a design on a board
A short written story beside each piece explains the thinking behind the work.
The three-part structure
The case study structure
Problem: what was needed
Process: what you did
Result: what happened
Every case study follows this order, so a busy viewer can find each part quickly.
Part
Questions to answer
Typical length
Title
What was it, and for whom (type of customer)?
One line
Problem (or brief)
What did the customer need? What made it challenging: budget, deadline, size, special request?
2 to 3 sentences
Process
What steps did you take? What choices did you make and why? What was your part if it was team work?
3 to 5 sentences or bullet points

What did you deliver? What happened afterwards: numbers, feedback, repeat orders?

For a beginner portfolio, about **150 to 300 words** per main case study is enough. Your one or two most important pieces can be longer, and smaller pieces can have just three short lines, one for each part.
Writing each part well
**Be specific.** "A 3-tier cake for 120 guests, delivered 90 km away" says more than "a big wedding cake".
**Show your thinking.** Explain one or two choices: why you used that fabric, why you chose those colours, why you planned a back-up.
**Use plain words.** Write as you would explain it to a customer on the phone.
**Honest results only.** If you do not know the exact numbers, use what you do know: the customer's words, a repeat order, the date it was delivered on time.
**Write in the first person.** "I measured", "I suggested": it is your story.
Worked example: a full case study for a cake order
For example, Bisi is a baker in Lagos. This is the case study she writes for her first portfolio piece, about 170 words long.
Title: "Football-themed 2-tier birthday cake for a 7-year-old's party, Ikeja".
Problem: "A mother wanted a cake in her son's club colours for 40 children, delivered in 4 days. The party was outdoors in the afternoon, so buttercream decorations risked melting."

Process: "I suggested a sponge with a firmer fondant covering instead of soft buttercream. I made the football and jersey toppers two days ahead so they could dry hard. I sent her a sketch and a photo of the colour samples on WhatsApp for approval before baking. I delivered in a cool box and set it up in the shade."
Result: "The cake stayed firm through the 3-hour party. The mother wrote: 'The children screamed when they saw it, and it tasted as good as it looked.' She has since ordered two more cakes."
In under a minute a new customer learns that Bisi handles deadlines, thinks about heat, communicates before baking and gets repeat orders. No photo alone could show all that.
A non-physical example

The same structure works for work you cannot photograph. A virtual assistant might write: Problem: "A shop owner's customer orders were lost across three WhatsApp chats." Process: "I set up a Google Sheet order log with columns for date, item, amount, payment status and delivery, and trained her two staff in a 30-minute session." Result: "After one month, she told me no order had been missed. She now uses the sheet daily." Add a screenshot of the sheet with sample data, never the real customer details.
Collect results while they are fresh

At delivery, ask: "How did it go? Can I quote you?" A week later, ask if anything changed: more customers, fewer complaints, compliments from guests. Save the replies in your Testimonials folder. Results you collect at the time are far easier and more accurate than results you try to remember months later.
Using testimonials well

A testimonial is stronger when it is short, specific and clearly from a real person. Quote the customer's words exactly, correcting only spelling, and add their first name, the type of job and the town, for example "Tolu, office lunch packs for 30 staff, Yaba". Put the testimonial at the end of the result section, where it confirms what you have just described. Do not write testimonials yourself and attach a customer's name.
Common mistakes to avoid
Writing only about yourself ("I am passionate and creative") instead of the customer's need.

A portfolio works because people believe it. Every piece of evidence you show is a promise: "This is what I can do for you." If a customer finds that one piece was not really yours, or a result was exaggerated, she stops believing everything else. Honesty is not only right; it is what makes a portfolio valuable. The honest portfolio rules
**Your work only.** Every image shows work you made or substantially contributed to.
**Name your part.** In team work, state your role clearly.
**True results.** Numbers and outcomes you can support with messages, records or the customer's word.
**True images.** Edits can fix light and crop clutter, but must not change the item: no adding beads, smoothing seams or changing colour.
**Label AI images.** If you use an AI tool to make a mock-up, say so. Never present AI-generated pictures as photos of products you made.
**Permission and privacy.** As in Module 1: written permission and no private details.

Once your portfolio is public, some people may ask you to do a "small test" before they hire you. Sometimes this is genuine, especially for jobs. Sometimes it is a way to collect free work from many people. Your portfolio exists to make most free tests unnecessary: the evidence is already there.
Worked example: responding to a test request
For example, Oluchi, a graphic designer, gets a message: "We like your portfolio. Before we pay, design our full logo and five flyers as a test. If we like it we will hire you."
Oluchi notes that a full logo and five flyers is the actual job, not a test.

She replies politely: "Thank you. My portfolio has six case studies, including two logo projects for small businesses. I am happy to do a short paid first stage: three logo ideas for approximately ₦15,000, which goes towards the full price if you continue."
She offers instead to answer questions about how she would approach their brief.
The person stops replying.
Oluchi kept her time and her ideas. A genuine client usually accepts a small paid first stage or relies on the portfolio, and someone collecting free designs moves on.

If you do agree to a test for a job application, keep it small (for example, one flyer, not a whole campaign), put your name on it, and send a low-resolution or watermarked version until there is an agreement.

Because portfolios are public, you may one day see your photos on another seller's page. Stay calm and collect evidence first: screenshots with the date, the link, and your original photo file, which has the original date and full size. Then message the person politely and ask them to remove it. Most large platforms, including Instagram, Facebook and Behance, have a way to report content that uses your work without permission. Your organised portfolio folder with original files is your best evidence.

The five-second test

Show someone your home page for five seconds, then hide it. Ask: "What do I do? Who is it for? How would you contact me?" If they cannot answer all three, your headline, first image or contact button needs work. This simple test reveals more than a long discussion.
The stranger review

Ask two or three people who are like your customers, but who do not know your work well, to look at the whole portfolio on their phone. Give them specific questions instead of asking whether they like it:
Which piece did you remember most, and why?
Was there any piece you thought was weaker than the others?
Was there anything confusing, or any word you did not understand?
If you needed this service, what would stop you from contacting me?
Did any page load slowly or look strange on your phone?
Listen, do not defend
When someone gives feedback, write it down and say thank you. Do not explain or argue. If two or more people say the same thing, treat it as a real problem to fix.
Turning feedback into changes

Write every comment in a simple list, then sort it into three groups. **Fix now:** problems two or more people noticed, or anything that stops contact, such as a broken button. **Consider:** single opinions about taste, such as a colour someone disliked; think about them, but you do not have to act. **Ignore politely:** comments that would take you away from your goal, such as "You should also add your wedding work" when your goal is children's parties. Then make the fixes one at a time and re-check the page on your phone after each change.

Be careful with feedback from people who are not your customers. A fellow designer may care about fonts, while your real customers care about whether the cake arrives on time. Give more weight to people who resemble the person in your portfolio goal sentence.

Writing your About section

Keep it short, warm and relevant: three to five sentences. Say who you are, what you do, how long you have done it, any relevant training, and what customers can expect working with you. Add, replace or remove?

Each time you consider a new piece, use the quality and relevance test from Module 1 again. A new piece should go in only if it is at least as strong and relevant as the weakest piece already there. For example, Grace, the bead maker from Module 2, does her first quarterly review three months after launching. Her portfolio has six pieces.

Keep a short change log, either as a note at the bottom of your planning document or a line in your tracker, recording the date and what you changed. After a year, this log, together with your enquiry tracker, shows clearly which changes brought more customers and which made no difference. It also makes it easy to undo a change that did not work.

Phones are lost, stolen or damaged, and free accounts can be locked if you forget a password. Light is the most important thing. Place the item close to a window, with light coming from the side. Side light shows stitching, beading and icing.
Hold a sheet of white paper or a white plate on the dark side to soften the shadows. Keep the background plain.
Avoid harsh midday sun, which makes hard shadows. Turn off yellow ceiling bulbs, because mixed light gives strange colours.
And do not use the flash. It flattens texture and makes shiny spots on soap, glass or satin.
Shot list
Four photos for every piece
Edit lightly. Colours must stay true to the real item.
Overall: the whole item, straight on
Detail: the part that shows your skill
Scale: a hand or object to show size
In use: worn, served or displayed
Wipe the lens first, because finger grease makes photos hazy. Then take an overall shot of the whole item, filling most of the frame.
Next a detail shot, close up on a hem, beadwork or piping. Tap the screen on the item to focus, and move closer instead of zooming.
Then a scale shot, like a hand holding the item, so the viewer knows its size.
Finally an in-use shot: the item worn, served or displayed. Take several of each, and keep the sharpest.
When you edit, crop and brighten a little only. If the fabric is wine, it must look wine, not red. No beauty filters on hair or makeup work.

Why it matters
Good work is not enough on its own
Most visitors use a phone
They give up if it is confusing
Trust breaks with one false piece
Track what brings enquiries
A portfolio with excellent work can still lose customers. Most visitors open your link on a phone, often on a slow connection, and they give up quickly if the page is confusing.
Every piece you show is a promise. If one piece is not really yours, a customer stops believing everything else.
And you need to know whether your portfolio actually brings enquiries, so you improve it on evidence, not guesses.
Structure
Five sections, best work first
Home: name, headline, best piece, contact
Work: 5 to 8 pieces, strongest first
About: short story and a photo at work
Services: what you offer, prices from
Contact: WhatsApp, email, area, hours

Start with Home: your name, a headline, your best piece and a contact button. A good headline says what you do, for whom, and where. For example, bridal and event makeup for brides in Kano and nearby.
Then Work: your five to eight pieces, strongest first, each with a clear title like Bridal makeup, outdoor wedding, Kano, not Project 3.
About: a short paragraph and a friendly photo of you at work.
Services, with starting prices if you choose to share them. And Contact. If you are just starting, these can all be sections on one long page, which loads faster on phones.
One-tap contact
Build a WhatsApp click-to-chat link
Test the link on two phones before you share it.
Write your number: 0803 123 4567
Drop the first 0, add 234 in front
Link: https://wa.me/2348031234567
Add a Chat on WhatsApp button in 3 places
Most Nigerian customers prefer WhatsApp. A click-to-chat link opens a chat with you without saving your number. For example, Halima's number is 0803 123 4567, an illustrative number.
She removes the first zero and adds Nigeria's country code, 234. No plus sign, no spaces.
Her link is w a dot m e, slash, then that full number. She can even add a ready message that appears in the chat box.
She adds a Chat on WhatsApp button to her home, work and services sections, so a visitor can reach her with one tap from anywhere.
Then she tests it on her own phone and a friend's phone. Also open your whole site on mobile data, tap every button, and zoom into the photos.
Honesty
Honest
Misleading
Edits may improve the photo. Cropping clutter, brightening and straightening are fine.
But if the customer would receive something different from the photo, the edit is misleading. And if you use an AI tool for a mock-up, say so. Never pass it off as a real product.
Protect your money
A 'client' pays too much and asks for the difference back. Do not send. Check your bank app, not an SMS.
Nobody needs your OTP, card PIN or BVN to pay you. Refuse. If you shared one, call your bank at once.
A full logo and five flyers is the job, not a test. Offer a small paid first stage instead.

Once your work is public, watch for three dangers. First, a client who sends more than the price and asks you to send back the difference. Do not send money back. Confirm the payment in your bank app, not a screenshot or SMS alert.
Second, anyone asking for your OTP, card PIN or BVN to pay you. Refuse. If you shared an OTP by mistake, call your bank's official customer care number at once.

Third, a large free test. For example, Oluchi was asked for a full logo and five flyers as a test. She offered three logo ideas for approximately 15,000 naira, going towards the full price. The person stopped replying, and she kept her ideas.
Track enquiries
Ask: how did you find me?
For example, a caterer's tracker records each enquiry, where it came from, and its value.
Tolu, lunch packs, portfolio link
Bimpe, cake, link in Instagram bio
Figures are illustrative.

Before tracking, test. Show someone your home page for five seconds, then hide it. Ask: what do I do, who is it for, how would you contact me? Then ask every new enquirer one question: how did you find me? Write the answer in a notebook or a free Google Sheet.

For example, Tolu found the portfolio link on WhatsApp status and booked lunch packs worth 45,000 naira. Bimpe found the link in an Instagram bio and ordered a cake worth 30,000. These figures are illustrative.
Each month, review your tracker and change one thing at a time, so you can see what made the difference. Enquiries and jobs matter more than views.

To remember. Put what you do, for whom and where at the top. Make contact one tap, and test it. Never let an edit change the item.
Never share your OTP, PIN or BVN. And track every enquiry, changing one thing at a time.

Why it matters
Finished, seen and kept current
Many portfolios never launch
Nobody can hire from a hidden link
An old portfolio looks abandoned
The most common reason portfolios never launch is that the project drags on for months. A short plan fixes that.
A portfolio that nobody opens cannot bring you work, so the link must go where your customers already are.
And a portfolio last updated two years ago tells a visitor you may have stopped working. Small, regular updates keep it alive.
About an hour a day
Your seven-day build plan
Done is better than perfect. Publish when the checklist passes.
Days 1 to 2: confirm pieces, final photos
Days 3 to 4: case studies and testimonials
Day 5: build all five sections
Day 6: phone test, five-second test, audit
Day 7: publish, test on two phones, share
Days 1 and 2. Confirm your 5 to 8 pieces in order, and re-photograph any weak ones, so each has 3 to 4 good photos.
Days 3 and 4. Write case studies of 150 to 300 words for your top three pieces, and three short lines for the rest.
Day 5. Build Home, Work, About, Services and Contact. Keep About to three to five warm sentences, with a real photo of you at work.
Day 6. Run the phone test, the five-second test and the honesty audit, and fix what fails.
Day 7. Publish, check the link on two phones, and save it in a note so you can paste it in seconds. If you miss a day, just continue the next day.
Remember, six good pieces published are worth far more than a perfect portfolio sitting unfinished on your phone.
Share once, work forever
Instagram, Facebook and TikTok bios
Your email signature
Your CV and LinkedIn Featured section
A QR code on cards and labels
Set your link up once in these places. The free WhatsApp Business app lets you add a website link to your profile. Customers see it when they tap your name.
Put it in every social media bio.
Add it to your Gmail signature, so it appears under every email.
Put it near the top of your CV, and in your LinkedIn Featured section if you are looking for jobs.
Canva can make a free QR code for business cards and flyers. Test the printed code on two phones before printing many copies. And once it is printed, keep the same link.
Introduce it well
Never send a bare link
Weak
A link with no words
Looks like spam
People fear clicking it
Strong
Who you are and why you write
What they will see
A clear next step
A link with no explanation looks like spam, and many people are rightly careful about unknown links.

For example, Amaka replies to a price enquiry: here are six of my children's birthday cakes, with what each customer asked for. Themed cakes start from approximately 35,000 naira. What theme does your child love?
A reason to click, what they will see, and a next step.
Quarterly review
Grace keeps her prices current
For example, Grace the bead maker reviews her portfolio three months after launch.
Old guide: bridal sets from
New guide after supplier rise
Naira prices are approximate.
Here is a quarterly review. Grace's tracker shows 18 enquiries in three months. 11 mentioned the portfolio, and most asked about bridal bead sets.
So she swaps her two weakest everyday necklaces for two stronger bridal sets, and puts the best bridal set first. She also changes her headline to bridal and occasion bead sets.
Her old price guide said bridal sets from approximately 18,000 naira.
Her bead supplier raised prices, so she updates it to approximately 22,000, and saves a PDF of the old and new versions.
Keep it working
Your update routine
After each good job: photos, permission, 3 lines
Monthly: check tracker, swap a weaker piece
Every 3 months: full review, prices, links
New piece replaces the weakest one
Back up to Google Drive
Two-step verification on

After every good job, take photos, ask permission and a testimonial, and write three lines. That takes 15 to 20 minutes. Monthly, check your tracker and buttons. Every three months, read it all as a stranger and update prices and links.
A new piece goes in only if it is as strong as your weakest one, and then it replaces it. That keeps your selection tight.

Protect it too. Keep originals in Google Drive, use a password you use nowhere else, and turn on two-step verification. If someone takes over your account, they can change your contact button to their own number.
